title: Reading & Phonics
description: Learn to read from the ground up: letter sounds, blending, word families, sight words, and the tricky letter teams that unlock thousands of words. Then put it all together with fluent reading and real comprehension skills like retelling and finding the main idea.
outcomes: You can say the sound for every letter and tell vowels from consonants.
You can blend sounds together to read short words like sun, map, and fish.
You can read words with magic e, vowel teams, and bossy r, like cake, boat, and bird.
You can read common sight words like the, said, and was without sounding them out.
You can break a big word into syllables and read it chunk by chunk.
You can retell a story with its characters, setting, problem, and solution.

units.title: Letters and Sounds
units.summary: Every letter has a name and at least one sound. This unit builds the sound-to-letter connections that all reading is built on.

lessons.title: Letter Names and Letter Sounds
lessons.intro: Here is the biggest secret of reading: letters are pictures of sounds. The letter name is what you call it, but the letter sound is what it says inside a word. Once you know the sounds, you can figure out words you have never seen before.

sections.heading: Names Are Not Sounds
body: The alphabet has 26 letters, and every letter has two jobs. Its **name** is what you say when you sing the alphabet song: ay, bee, see. Its **sound** is what it says in a word. The letter m is named em, but in the word map it just says /m/, like the start of a hum.

When you read, you use sounds, not names. If you tried to read the word cat with letter names, you would say see-ay-tee, which is not a word at all. With sounds, you say /k/ /a/ /t/, and there it is: cat.
Practice this way: point to a letter, say its name, then say its sound. Keep the sound short and clean. The letter b says /b/, not buh. Adding uh to the end makes blending much harder later.

sections.heading: Vowels and Consonants
body: Five letters are special: **a, e, i, o, u**. These are the **vowels**, and every word in English needs at least one. Your mouth stays open when you say a vowel sound. Try saying the a in apple and feel how the air flows out freely.
All the other letters are **consonants**. When you say a consonant sound, some part of your mouth blocks the air: your lips for /b/ and /p/, your tongue for /t/ and /d/, your teeth and lip for /f/.
The letter y is a helper. At the start of a word it is a consonant, like in yes. At the end it often acts like a vowel, saying /ee/ in happy or /igh/ in fly.

example.problem: Sort these letters into vowels and consonants: t, e, s, o, m, a
steps: Remember the vowel list: a, e, i, o, u.
Check each letter against the list: e, o, and a are on it.
Everything else is a consonant: t, s, and m.
example.answer: Vowels: e, o, a. Consonants: t, s, m.

keyTerms.def: What you call a letter when you say the alphabet, like em for m.
What a letter says inside a word, like /m/ in map.
One of the open-mouth letters: a, e, i, o, u, and sometimes y.
Any letter that is not a vowel; its sound blocks the air somewhere in your mouth.

practice.q: Which letter is a vowel?
practice.explain: The vowels are a, e, i, o, and u. The letter e is on that list; b, t, and s are consonants.

practice.q: What sound does the letter m say in the word map?
practice.explain: In a word we use the letter's sound, /m/, not its name em. Keep the sound short, with no uh added.

practice.q: Why does every word need a vowel?
choices: English words must have at least one open-mouth sound
Vowels come first in the alphabet
practice.explain: Every English word and every syllable has at least one vowel sound, the open-mouth sound that carries the word.

lessons.title: Consonants at Work
lessons.intro: Consonants are the sturdy walls of words, and most of them are wonderfully reliable: b almost always says /b/, and t almost always says /t/. Learn the reliable ones well, and note the few tricksters, and you can attack most short words with confidence.

sections.heading: The Reliable Consonants
body: Most consonants say one sound almost every time: b as in bat, d as in dog, f as in fish, m as in mop, n as in net, p as in pig, t as in top. When you see these letters, you can trust them.

Say each sound crisply and quickly. Sounds like /t/ and /p/ are quick pops of air. Sounds like /m/, /n/, /s/, and /f/ can be stretched out: mmmm, ssss. Stretchy sounds are great for beginners because you can hold them while you think about the next letter.
A good daily drill: an adult or partner points to a consonant, and you say its sound in under one second. Speed matters, because reading a word means saying its sounds one right after another.

sections.heading: The Tricksters: c, g, and Friends
body: The letter c has two sounds. Usually it says /k/ as in cat and cup. But before e, i, or y it usually says /s/, as in city and race. The letter g works the same way: /g/ in goat, but often /j/ before e, i, or y, as in giant and gym.

The letter x usually says /ks/ at the end of words, like box and fox, which is really two sounds squeezed together. The letter q almost never travels alone; it brings u along and the pair says /kw/, as in queen and quick.
Do not try to memorize every rule at once. Start by trusting the common sound, and when a word sounds wrong, try the trickster's second sound. Good readers flex like this all the time.

example.problem: Which sound does c make in the word city?
steps: Look at the letter right after the c. It is i.
Remember the rule: c before e, i, or y usually says /s/.
Test it: /s/ /i/ /t/ /ee/ sounds like city. That works.

keyTerms.def: The /k/ sound of c, as in cat and cup.
The /s/ sound of c before e, i, or y, as in city.
The /g/ sound of g, as in goat.
The /j/ sound of g before e, i, or y, as in giant.

practice.q: Which word uses the soft c sound /s/?
practice.explain: In race, the c comes before e, so it says /s/. In cat, cup, and cot, c says its usual hard sound /k/.

practice.q: What two sounds does x make at the end of box?
practice.explain: The letter x at the end of a word says /ks/, which is the /k/ sound followed quickly by /s/.

practice.q: Which letter almost always brings u along with it?
practice.explain: The letter q nearly always appears as qu, and together the pair says /kw/, as in queen.

lessons.title: Short Vowels
lessons.intro: Vowels are shape-shifters, but their short sounds come first and matter most: thousands of small words like cat, bed, pig, top, and bug use them. Master these five sounds and you can read whole sentences of real words.

sections.heading: The Five Short Sounds
body: Each vowel has a short sound with a keyword to anchor it: a as in **apple**, e as in **elephant**, i as in **igloo**, o as in **octopus**, u as in **umbrella**. Say the keyword, then peel off just the first sound: apple gives you /a/.

Short e and short i are the easiest pair to mix up. Say bed and then bid slowly and feel your mouth: it opens a little wider for /e/. If a word sounds almost right but not quite, try swapping between these two.
When a word has just one vowel with consonants around it, like hat or bug, the vowel usually says its short sound. Teachers call these **CVC words**: consonant, vowel, consonant.

example.problem: Read the word 'hot' using the short vowel sound.
steps: Find the vowel. It is o, sitting between two consonants, so expect the short sound.
Anchor the sound with the keyword: octopus starts with /o/.
Say the three sounds in order: /h/ /o/ /t/.
Blend them together smoothly: hot.
example.answer: hot, with o saying its short sound as in octopus

sections.heading: Hearing the Middle Sound
body: The middle vowel is the hardest sound to hear in a word, because the consonants at the edges grab your attention. Train your ear with sound stretching: say cat very slowly, caaaat, and listen for the /a/ hiding in the middle.
Try minimal pairs, which are words that differ by one sound: cat and cot, pin and pen, big and bag. Say each pair out loud and name which vowel changed. This sharpens the exact skill reading needs.
A helpful home activity: gather small objects or pictures such as a cap, a pen, a pig, a mop, and a cup, and sort them into five piles by their middle vowel sound. Ears first, letters second.

keyTerms.def: The quick vowel sound, like /a/ in apple or /o/ in octopus.
A consonant-vowel-consonant word like cat or bug, where the vowel is usually short.
An anchor word that starts with a sound, used to remember it, like igloo for short i.
Two words that differ by exactly one sound, like pin and pen.

practice.q: Which word has the short a sound, as in apple?
practice.explain: Cat is a CVC word, so its a says the short sound /a/. Cake, day, and rain all use the long a sound.

practice.q: Which vowel sound is in the middle of the word bug?
practice.explain: Stretch it out: buuug. The middle sound is /u/ as in umbrella, so bug has short u.

practice.q: The words pin and pen are different because of which sound?
practice.explain: Both start with /p/ and end with /n/. Only the middle vowel changes: short i in pin, short e in pen.

units.title: Building Words
units.summary: Now the sounds snap together. You will blend sounds into words, use word families to read whole groups at once, and handle consonant blends.

lessons.title: Blending Sounds into Words
lessons.intro: Blending is the moment reading actually happens: you say each sound, slide them together, and a word pops out of your mouth. It feels like magic the first time, but it is a skill, and skills grow with the right kind of practice.

sections.heading: Slide, Don't Chop
body: Beginners often chop sounds apart: /s/ ... /u/ ... /n/, with big gaps. Then the word gets lost in the silence. The fix is **continuous blending**: hold each sound and slide straight into the next with no gap at all, like ssssuuuunnnn. Then say it fast: sun.

Start with words whose first sound can be stretched, like m, s, f, n, l, and r. Words like sun, map, fan, and lip blend smoothly. Save popping sounds like /b/, /t/, and /k/ for a little later, since you cannot stretch a pop.
Touch and slide helps too: put a finger under each letter as you say its sound, then sweep your finger under the whole word as you say it fast. Your hand teaches your voice what to do.

example.problem: Blend the sounds /m/ /a/ /p/ into a word.
steps: Say the first sound and hold it: mmmm.
Slide into the vowel without stopping: mmmaaaa.
Add the last sound: mmmaaap.
Now say it at normal speed: map.

sections.heading: Taking Words Apart
body: The reverse skill is **segmenting**: hearing a whole word and breaking it into its sounds. Say dog, then tap once for each sound: /d/ /o/ /g/, three taps. Segmenting is exactly how spelling works, so this practice pays off twice.
Count sounds, not letters. The word fish has four letters but only three sounds: /f/ /i/ /sh/. For now, stick to simple words like sat, red, and mud where letters and sounds match one to one.
Make it physical: say a word, then move one small block or coin forward for each sound you hear. Then touch each block and say its sound again. Then sweep them together and say the word.

keyTerms.def: Sliding sounds together to read a word, like /s/ /u/ /n/ becoming sun.
Breaking a spoken word into its separate sounds, the key skill for spelling.
Blending with no gaps between sounds: ssssuuuunnnn, then sun.

practice.q: Blend these sounds: /s/ /i/ /t/. What word do they make?
practice.explain: The middle sound is short i as in igloo, so the sounds slide together into sit.

practice.q: How many sounds are in the spoken word dog?
practice.explain: Tap it out: /d/ /o/ /g/ is three sounds, one for each letter in this word.

practice.q: Which word is easiest to blend for a beginner, and why?
choices: sun, because its first sound can be stretched
practice.explain: You can hold /s/ as ssss and slide into the vowel with no gap. Popping sounds like /t/, /k/, and /b/ cannot be stretched, which makes gaps more likely.

lessons.title: Word Families
lessons.intro: Learn to read cat, and you are one letter swap away from hat, bat, sat, mat, and rat. Word families let you read in bulk: master one ending chunk and dozens of words come free.

sections.heading: One Chunk, Many Words
body: A **word family** is a group of words that share the same ending chunk, called a **rime**. The -at family includes cat, hat, bat, sat, and flat. The first part of the word, the sound or sounds before the vowel, is called the **onset**.
Reading by families is faster than blending sound by sound. Once your brain owns the chunk -at, you read hat by snapping /h/ onto at. That is one move instead of three.
The most useful early families include -at, -an, -ap, -en, -et, -ig, -in, -op, -ot, -ug, and -un. Notice they cover all five short vowels, so family practice is also vowel practice.

example.problem: Use the -op family to read the word 'mop'.
steps: Spot the family chunk at the end: op, which says /op/ as in top.
Find the onset, the letter before the chunk: m, which says /m/.
Snap them together: /m/ + /op/.
Say it as one word: mop.

sections.heading: Rhyme Time
body: Words in the same family rhyme, so rhyming games build reading power. Say a word like bug and take turns naming rhymes: rug, hug, mug, tug. Silly made-up words like zug are fine; the ear training is what counts.

Try word ladders: start with cat, change one letter at a time, and see where you climb. Cat becomes bat, bat becomes bag, bag becomes big. Each rung asks you to notice exactly which sound and letter changed.
When you meet a new word while reading, check whether you already know its family. A reader who owns -ing can handle king, ring, sing, and even bring without slowing down.

keyTerms.def: A group of words sharing the same ending chunk, like cat, hat, and bat.
The vowel and everything after it in a syllable, like -at in cat.
The consonant sound or sounds before the vowel, like c- in cat.
When two words end with the same sounds, like bug and rug.

practice.q: Which word belongs to the -at family?
practice.explain: Hat ends with the chunk -at, so it rhymes with cat and bat. Hit, hot, and heat have different vowel sounds.

practice.q: In the word sun, what is the onset?
practice.explain: The onset is everything before the vowel. In sun that is just /s/. The rime is -un.

practice.q: You can read 'ring'. Which new word does the same family unlock?
practice.explain: Sing shares the -ing chunk with ring, so you snap /s/ onto -ing. Rain, rang, and grin use different chunks.

lessons.title: Blends at the Beginning and End
lessons.intro: What happens when two consonants stand side by side, like the st in stop or the mp in lamp? In a blend, you can still hear both sounds; they just come out fast, back to back. Blends turn three-sound words into four-sound words, and your ears are ready.

sections.heading: Beginning Blends
body: A **consonant blend** is two or three consonants together where every sound is still heard. In stop you can hear both /s/ and /t/: /s/ /t/ /o/ /p/, four sounds. Compare that to sock, which starts with just one consonant sound.

Common beginning blends come in groups: s-blends like st, sn, sp, sw (stop, snap, spin, swim), l-blends like bl, cl, fl, pl (blue, clap, flag, plum), and r-blends like br, cr, dr, tr (brag, crab, drip, trip).
To read a blend word, do not treat the blend as a mystery chunk. Just blend all the sounds in order, the same way you always do. The only change is that there is one more sound to slide through.

steps: Spot the beginning blend fl: two consonants, both heard.
Say all four sounds in order: /f/ /l/ /a/ /g/.
Slide them together with no gaps: fflllaaag.
Say it fast: flag.

sections.heading: Ending Blends
body: Blends live at the ends of words too: -nd in hand, -mp in lamp, -st in nest, -nt in tent, -sk in desk. Ending blends are sneaky because the two sounds rush by quickly, so slow the word down when you spell it: haaannnd.
A word like stamp has a blend at both ends: /s/ /t/ /a/ /m/ /p/, five sounds in a one-syllable word. If you can tap out stamp, your sound skills are getting strong.
Careful: a blend is not the same as a digraph. In a blend like st you hear two sounds. In a digraph like sh, two letters team up to make one brand-new sound. Digraphs get their own lesson next.

keyTerms.def: Two or three consonants together where each sound is still heard, like st in stop.
A blend starting with s, like sn in snap or sw in swim.
A blend at the end of a word, like -mp in lamp or -nd in hand.

practice.q: How many sounds are in the word stop?
practice.explain: Tap it: /s/ /t/ /o/ /p/. The blend st keeps both of its sounds, so stop has four.

practice.q: Which word ends with a consonant blend?
practice.explain: Hand ends with -nd, and you can hear both /n/ and /d/. Cat ends with a single consonant sound.

practice.q: Which word has a blend at the beginning AND the end?
practice.explain: Stamp starts with the blend st and ends with the blend mp: five sounds total. Trap only has a beginning blend.

units.title: Letter Teams
units.summary: Sometimes letters team up to make one new sound, and sometimes a silent letter changes everything. This unit covers digraphs, magic e, vowel teams, and bossy r.

lessons.title: Digraphs: sh, ch, th, wh, ck
lessons.intro: Say ship. That first sound, /sh/, does not belong to s or to h; the two letters team up to make one totally new sound. Letter teams like this are called digraphs, and five of them unlock a huge number of everyday words.

sections.heading: Two Letters, One Sound
body: A **digraph** is two letters that make a single sound. The big four at the start of words are **sh** as in ship, **ch** as in chip, **th** as in thin, and **wh** as in whale. Say chip and notice you cannot hear a /k/ or an /h/ anywhere; ch is its own sound.

The digraph **th** actually has two versions. In thin, thumb, and math it is quiet, just air between your teeth. In the, this, and that it buzzes; put your fingers on your throat and feel the hum. Both are spelled th, and your mouth usually picks the right one automatically.
The team **ck** appears at the end of short words right after a short vowel, and it simply says /k/: duck, sock, back, kick. It never starts a word.

example.problem: How many sounds are in the word fish?
steps: Look for letter teams first: sh at the end is a digraph, one sound.
Count the sounds in order: /f/, /i/, /sh/.
Four letters, but the sh counts as one.

sections.heading: Spotting Teams Before You Blend
body: Good readers scan a word for letter teams before sounding it out. If you blend ship as /s/ /h/ /i/ /p/, you get a nonsense word. Spot the sh first, treat it as one sound, and the word reads cleanly.
A useful drill is digraph hunting: take a page from any book and circle every sh, ch, th, wh, and ck you can find in one minute. The faster your eyes find teams, the smoother your reading gets.

Remember the difference from the last lesson: in a blend like st you hear both sounds, but in a digraph like sh the letters melt into one new sound. Ask yourself: can I hear each letter? If not, it is a digraph.

keyTerms.def: Two letters that make one new sound, like sh in ship.
The buzzing th in the and this; your throat vibrates.
The quiet, airy th in thin and math.
The team that says /k/ after a short vowel at the end of words like duck.

practice.q: Which word begins with a digraph?
practice.explain: Ship starts with sh, two letters making the single sound /sh/. Stop and slip start with blends, where both sounds are heard.

practice.q: How many sounds are in the word chick?
practice.explain: Both ch and ck are digraphs, one sound each: /ch/ /i/ /k/. Five letters, three sounds.

practice.q: In which word does th buzz, with your throat vibrating?
practice.explain: This uses voiced th; touch your throat and feel the hum. Thin, math, and thumb use the quiet, airy th.

lessons.title: Magic E
lessons.intro: Add one silent letter to the end of cap and it becomes cape. Add it to kit and you get kite. The e at the end says nothing itself, but it reaches back over one consonant and makes the vowel say its own name. Readers call it magic e.

sections.heading: How the Magic Works
body: A **long vowel** is a vowel that says its own name: a in cape, i in kite, o in rope, u in cube. The **magic e** pattern (also called silent e) is vowel, consonant, then e: a_e, i_e, o_e, u_e. The final e is silent, and the first vowel goes long.

Watch the transformations: cap → cape, kit → kite, hop → hope, cub → cube, tap → tape, pin → pine. In each pair the middle vowel flips from its short sound to its name. One silent letter, a whole new word.

When you meet a word ending in e, check the pattern: is there exactly one consonant between a vowel and that final e? If yes, try the long vowel first. So note reads with a long o, but nod, with no e, keeps its short o.

steps: Scan the ending: it fits the magic e pattern i_e (i, then d, then silent e).
The e is silent, and it makes the i say its name: /igh/.
Blend the sounds: /r/ /igh/ /d/.
Say it smoothly: ride.
example.answer: ride, with a long i and a silent e

sections.heading: Practicing the Flip
body: Play the flip game with word pairs. Write cap, read it, then add an e and read cape. Do the same with rob and robe, tub and tube, plan and plane. Saying both words out loud, back to back, locks in what the e does.

There are a few common exceptions where the vowel stays short even with a final e, such as have, give, love, and come. These show up so often that you will simply learn them as sight words in the next unit.
Magic e also explains spelling choices. If you want to write the word hope, you need the e; write hop and you have said something quite different about that frog.

keyTerms.def: A vowel saying its own name, like the a in cape.
A final silent e that makes the earlier vowel say its name, as in kite.
The spelling shape a_e, i_e, o_e, or u_e that signals a long vowel.

practice.q: What happens when you add e to the end of 'kit'?
choices: It becomes kite, with a long i
practice.explain: The magic e pattern i_e makes the i say its name, turning kit into kite. The e itself stays silent.

practice.q: Which word has a long o sound?
practice.explain: Hope fits the o_e pattern, so the o says its name. Hop, hot, and top have no final e, so their o stays short.

practice.q: Which word is an exception where the vowel stays short despite the final e?
practice.explain: Give ends in e but keeps its short i sound. It is a common exception best learned by heart.

lessons.title: Vowel Teams and Bossy R
lessons.intro: Magic e is not the only way to make a long vowel. Pairs like ai, ee, and oa team up in rain, feet, and boat. And one letter, r, is so bossy that it changes any vowel standing in front of it. These two patterns finish your phonics toolkit.

sections.heading: Vowel Teams
body: A **vowel team** is two vowels working together to make one sound, usually the long sound of the first vowel. The classics: **ai** in rain, **ay** in play, **ee** in feet, **ea** in leaf, **oa** in boat. Many teachers say: when two vowels go walking, the first one does the talking.

The teams split up by position. In the middle of a word, use ai and oa: rain, train, boat, coat. At the end of a word, English prefers ay: play, day, stay. The team ee is happy anywhere: see, feet, tree.

The talking rule is a good first guess, not a law. The team ea usually says long e (leaf, team) but sometimes short e (bread, head). If your first try sounds wrong, flex the vowel sound and try again; that is what skilled readers do.

steps: Spot the vowel team oa in the middle.
The first vowel does the talking: o says its name, /oh/.
Blend: /b/ /oh/ /t/.
Say it smoothly: boat.
example.answer: boat, with oa saying long o

sections.heading: Bossy R
body: When r comes right after a vowel, it bosses the vowel around and changes its sound. **ar** says /ar/ as in car and star. **or** says /or/ as in corn and fork. These two are easy to hear and easy to trust.

Here is the surprise: **er**, **ir**, and **ur** all say the exact same sound, /er/. Her, bird, and fur rhyme in the middle even though they are spelled three different ways. For reading, that is great news: see any of the three, say /er/.
Bossy r words cannot be blended with a short vowel. If you try to read car as /k/ /a/ /r/ with a short a, it comes out wrong. Spot the vowel-plus-r chunk first and read it as one unit: /k/ /ar/.

keyTerms.def: Two vowels making one sound together, like oa in boat.
A vowel followed by r that changes sound, like ar in car.
The spellings er, ir, and ur, which all say the same /er/ sound.

practice.q: In the word rain, what sound does the team ai make?
practice.explain: In the team ai, the first vowel does the talking: a says its name, the long a sound.

practice.q: Which three spellings all say the same /er/ sound?
practice.explain: Her, bird, and fur prove it: er, ir, and ur are three spellings of one sound. Ar and or have their own distinct sounds.

practice.q: Which word ends the long a sound with the team ay?
practice.explain: At the end of a word, English usually spells long a with ay, as in play and day. Rain uses ai in the middle; pale uses magic e.

units.title: Words at a Glance
units.summary: Fast, smooth reading needs instant words and big-word strategies. Learn sight words, syllable chunking, and how to read with expression.

lessons.title: Sight Words
lessons.intro: Some words appear so often, and follow the rules so poorly, that the best move is to know them instantly by sight. Words like the, said, was, and of show up on nearly every page you will ever read. Own them, and every sentence gets easier.

sections.heading: Why Some Words Break the Rules
body: Try sounding out said letter by letter and you get something like sa-id, which is wrong; the word is actually pronounced sed. Words like said, was, of, one, and come are **irregular**: their spelling does not match their sound cleanly.

About 100 words make up roughly half of everything you read. Many are tiny glue words: the, a, to, and, is, you, it, was, for, on. Because they appear constantly, reading them instantly, without any sounding out, makes everything else flow.

Most sight words are only partly irregular. In said, the s and d behave perfectly; only the ai is odd. So do not just memorize the shape of the word. Notice which part follows the rules and which part is the troublemaker.

sections.heading: How to Learn Them
body: Learn a few at a time, five or so per week, not fifty at once. Read each word, spell it aloud, then use it in a spoken sentence: Was. W-a-s. The dog was muddy. Saying, spelling, and using beats silent staring.

Flashcards work best with quick, frequent rounds: two minutes, twice a day. Move a card to the mastered pile only after you have read it instantly three days in a row. Mix old cards back in so nothing fades.
Hunt for your words in the wild. Pick this week's five words and find them in a real book, on a cereal box, or on signs. Every real-world spotting is one more rep for your memory.

keyTerms.def: A word you recognize instantly without sounding it out.
A word whose spelling does not match its sound, like said or of.
A word that appears extremely often in print, like the and and.

practice.q: Which word is irregular and is best learned by sight?
practice.explain: Said is pronounced sed, so sounding out the ai fails. Sat, sad, and sit follow the short-vowel rules perfectly.

practice.q: Why are high-frequency words worth learning instantly?
choices: They appear in almost every sentence you read
practice.explain: A small set of about 100 words makes up around half of all print. Reading them instantly makes every page smoother.

practice.q: What is the smartest way to study the word said?
choices: Notice the s and d are regular and only the ai is odd
Sound it out letter by letter every time
practice.explain: Most irregular words are mostly regular. Anchoring the regular parts and flagging the odd part makes the word stick faster.

lessons.title: Chunking Big Words into Syllables
lessons.intro: The word watermelon looks scary until you see that it is just four small chunks: wa-ter-mel-on. Every big word is a train of syllables, and you already know how to read each car. Chunking is how strong readers stay calm around long words.

sections.heading: What a Syllable Is
body: A **syllable** is a beat of a word, and every syllable contains exactly one vowel sound. Clap as you say the beats: dog has one clap, ta-ble has two, ba-na-na has three, wa-ter-mel-on has four.

A quick trick: rest your hand flat under your chin and say the word. Your chin drops once for every syllable, because every vowel sound opens your mouth. Try it with elephant: el-e-phant, three drops.

Counting vowel sounds tells you how many chunks to expect. The word basket has two vowels, a and e, so expect two syllables: bas-ket. Silent letters do not count: cake has two vowel letters but only one vowel sound, so it is one syllable.

example.problem: How many syllables are in the word banana?
steps: Say it slowly and clap the beats: ba-na-na.
Count the claps: three.
Check with vowel sounds: /a/ appears three times, once per chunk.

sections.heading: Where to Split
body: The most common split is between two consonants in the middle: rab-bit, bas-ket, nap-kin, sis-ter. Each half becomes a small word you can blend the ordinary way, then you glue the halves together.

If a syllable ends in a consonant, like rab, its vowel is usually short. This is called a **closed syllable**. If it ends in a vowel, like the ta in ta-ble, the vowel is usually long. This is called an **open syllable**. Try me: it splits into two open chunks... actually just one syllable, me, and its e is long, exactly as the rule predicts.
Endings are chunks too. Spot -ing, -ed, -er, and -est, peel them off, read the base word, then stick the ending back on: jump-ing, fast-est. Big words stop being big once you see their seams.

keyTerms.def: One beat of a word, containing exactly one vowel sound.
A syllable ending in a consonant; its vowel is usually short, like rab in rabbit.
A syllable ending in a vowel; its vowel is usually long, like ta in table.
Breaking a long word into readable pieces, like wa-ter-mel-on.

practice.q: How many syllables are in the word elephant?
practice.explain: Clap it out: el-e-phant, three beats, and your chin drops three times when you say it.

practice.q: Where should you split the word rabbit?
practice.explain: Split between the two middle consonants: rab-bit. Each half is then easy to blend on its own.

practice.q: In the word table, why is the a long?
choices: Because ta is an open syllable ending in a vowel
practice.explain: Table splits as ta-ble. The first chunk ends in the vowel a, making it an open syllable, and open syllables usually have long vowels.

lessons.title: Reading with Fluency and Expression
lessons.intro: Reading every word correctly is not the finish line. Fluent reading sounds like talking: smooth, grouped into phrases, and full of expression. Fluency matters because a brain that is not fighting the words is free to enjoy the story.

sections.heading: Smooth, Not Fast
body: **Fluency** means reading accurately, at a comfortable speed, with expression. Notice what it does not mean: racing. A reader who speeds through, skipping words and ignoring periods, is less fluent than one who reads a bit slower but sounds natural.

Fluent readers group words into phrases instead of saying them one... at... a... time. Read this both ways: The little dog / ran down / the hill. Phrased reading sounds like speech and is far easier to understand.

The best fluency builder is **repeated reading**: read the same short passage three or four times across a few days. The first read is for accuracy; later reads get smoother and more expressive. Rereading a favorite book is real practice, not cheating.

sections.heading: Punctuation Is Your Script
body: Punctuation marks are stage directions. A period means stop briefly and let your voice fall. A comma means a small pause. A question mark makes your voice rise at the end: Are you coming? An exclamation point adds energy: Watch out!

Quotation marks mean a character is talking, so change your voice a little. When the story says the giant grumbled, let your voice grumble. Expression is not decoration; it shows that you understand what the words mean.

Try echo reading with a partner: the stronger reader reads a sentence with full expression, and you read the same sentence right after, matching the phrasing and tone. Your voice learns by imitation, just like it learned to talk.

keyTerms.def: Reading accurately, smoothly, and with expression, like natural talking.
Grouping words into meaningful chunks instead of reading word by word.
Reading the same passage several times to build smoothness.
Using your voice to match the meaning and feeling of the text.

practice.q: What should your voice do at a question mark?
practice.explain: Questions rise at the end, just like when you ask something out loud: Are you coming?

practice.q: Which reader is the most fluent?
choices: One who reads smoothly in phrases with expression
One who never pauses at periods
One who reads one word at a time perfectly
practice.explain: Fluency is accuracy plus comfortable speed plus expression. Racing and word-by-word reading both fall short.

practice.q: Why does rereading the same passage help?
choices: Each pass frees your brain to add smoothness and expression
practice.explain: Once the words are accurate, later reads can focus on phrasing and tone. Repeated reading is a proven fluency builder.

units.title: Understanding What You Read
units.summary: Decoding is only half the job; the point of reading is meaning. Learn to track story elements, retell in order, and read nonfiction like a detective.

lessons.title: Story Elements
lessons.intro: Almost every story is built from the same parts: someone (a character), somewhere (a setting), a problem, and a solution. When you can name these parts, stories stop being a blur of events and become a shape you recognize.

sections.heading: Who, Where, and When
body: The **characters** are who the story is about: people, animals, or even talking teapots. The **main character** is the one the story follows most closely, the one with the problem. Other characters help, cause trouble, or just pass through.

The **setting** is where and when the story happens: a farm at sunrise, a spaceship in the future, a school on the first day. Authors drop clues instead of announcements; snow, mittens, and hot cocoa tell you it is winter without saying so.
Try this with any story you know. In The Three Little Pigs, the main characters are the pigs, the troublemaker is the wolf, and the setting is the countryside where they build their houses.

sections.heading: Problem and Solution
body: The **problem** is what goes wrong or what the main character wants but cannot easily get. The **solution** is how it works out. In The Three Little Pigs, the problem is a wolf who blows houses down; the solution is the brick house he cannot beat.

Most stories follow a mountain shape: the beginning introduces characters and setting, the middle grows the problem bigger, and the ending delivers the solution. Knowing this shape tells you what to look for as you read.

While you read, pause and ask: what does the main character want right now, and what is standing in the way? If you can answer that, you understand the story engine. If you cannot, back up a page; something important slipped past.

example.problem: Read this mini-story and name its parts: Mia lost her kite at the park. She looked everywhere. Finally her brother spotted it stuck in a tall tree, and they got it down together.
steps: Who is the story mostly about? Mia. Her brother is a helper character.
Where does it happen? At the park; that is the setting.
What goes wrong? Mia's kite is lost. That is the problem.
How does it work out? Her brother finds it in a tree and they retrieve it: the solution.
example.answer: Main character: Mia. Setting: the park. Problem: the lost kite. Solution: finding it in the tree together.

keyTerms.def: A person or creature the story is about.
Where and when a story takes place.
What goes wrong or what the main character wants.
How the problem gets fixed by the end of the story.

practice.q: In the mini-story about Mia, what is the setting?
practice.explain: The story says Mia lost her kite at the park, so the park is where the story takes place.

practice.q: What is the problem in The Three Little Pigs?
choices: A wolf keeps blowing their houses down
practice.explain: The wolf destroying houses is what goes wrong; the brick house that stops him is the solution.

practice.q: Which question helps you find the main character?
choices: Who does the story follow most closely?
Who is on the last page?
practice.explain: The main character is the one the story tracks most and the one who faces the central problem.

lessons.title: Retelling and Making Predictions
lessons.intro: Can you tell a friend what a story was about, in order, in your own words? Retelling is the truest test of understanding. And guessing what comes next, called predicting, keeps your brain awake and hunting for clues while you read.

sections.heading: Retell in Order
body: A good **retelling** covers the beginning, the middle, and the end, in that order, in your own words. Use the signal words first, next, then, and finally to keep the events lined up: First Mia lost her kite. Then she searched. Finally her brother found it.

Retelling is not reciting. You do not repeat the book's exact sentences; you compress the story to its important events. Ask yourself: if my friend never read this book, what would they need to know to get it?

Use your hand as a five-finger checklist: thumb for characters, pointer for setting, middle for the problem, ring for the big events, pinky for the solution. Touch each finger as you retell and nothing important gets skipped.

sections.heading: Predict, Then Check
body: A **prediction** is a smart guess about what happens next, built from clues in the story plus what you already know. If a character walks out into dark clouds without a jacket, you might predict rain and a soggy character.

Predictions are not about being right; they are about being engaged. When you predict, you read on with a question burning: was I right? Wrong predictions are great, because noticing why you were wrong means you caught a detail you had missed.

Good moments to pause and predict: after the title and cover, when a problem appears, and right before the ending. Say your prediction out loud or jot one word, then read on and check it like a scientist checking an experiment.

keyTerms.def: Telling a story's important events in order, in your own words.
Order signals like first, next, then, and finally.
A smart guess about what happens next, based on clues.

practice.q: Which retelling of a story is in the correct shape?
choices: Beginning, middle, end, in order, in your own words
The exact words of the book, memorized
practice.explain: A retelling compresses the story into its key events, told in order and in your own words, not recited or scrambled.

practice.q: A character packs a swimsuit, a towel, and sunscreen. What is the best prediction?
choices: She is going to the library
practice.explain: Predictions come from clues. Swimsuit, towel, and sunscreen all point to swimming, probably somewhere sunny.

practice.q: Your prediction turned out wrong. What should you do?
choices: Notice which clue you misread and keep going
practice.explain: Wrong predictions are useful: figuring out why sharpens your attention to the story's real clues.

lessons.title: Reading Nonfiction
lessons.intro: Not every book tells a story. Nonfiction books give you true information about volcanoes, sharks, or space, and they come with special tools: headings, captions, bold words, and a glossary. Learn the tools and facts practically jump off the page.

sections.heading: Text Features Are Shortcuts
body: **Nonfiction** is writing about real things, meant to inform. Instead of characters and plot, it has **text features**: a table of contents to find chapters, **headings** that announce each section's topic, photos with **captions** that explain them, and **bold words** that flag important vocabulary.

At the back you may find a **glossary**, a mini-dictionary of the book's special words, and an **index**, an alphabetical list of topics with page numbers. Want to know what a book says about lava? The index sends you straight to the right pages.

Before reading a nonfiction book, take a feature walk: read the title, flip through the headings, look at pictures and captions. In two minutes you will know what the book covers and what you want to find out.

sections.heading: Facts, Opinions, and the Main Idea
body: A **fact** can be checked and proven: Honey never spoils. An **opinion** is what someone thinks or feels: Honey is the best snack. Words like best, worst, should, and beautiful are opinion flags. Good readers of nonfiction sort the two constantly.

The **main idea** is what a section is mostly about, and the **details** are the facts that support it. The heading usually points at the main idea. If the section is called What Bees Eat, every detail should connect to bee food.

After reading a section, test yourself: cover the page and state the main idea in one sentence, then recall two details. If you cannot, reread with the heading in mind. This little habit is how information actually sticks.

example.problem: Fact or opinion? (1) A ladybug has six legs. (2) Ladybugs are the cutest insects.
steps: Ask of each sentence: could we check and prove this?
Counting a ladybug's legs is checkable: six every time. That is a fact.
Cutest is a feeling word; people can disagree and nobody is provably wrong. That is an opinion.
example.answer: Sentence 1 is a fact; sentence 2 is an opinion.

keyTerms.def: Writing about real things, meant to inform.
A mini-dictionary at the back of a book explaining its special words.
A statement that can be checked and proven true.
What someone thinks or feels; it cannot be proven.
What a section of text is mostly about.

practice.q: Where would you look to find what the word larva means in a bug book?
practice.explain: The glossary is the book's mini-dictionary, defining the special words used inside.

practice.q: Which sentence is an opinion?
practice.explain: Coolest is a feeling word that cannot be proven. The other three statements can all be checked.

practice.q: A section is titled How Frogs Grow. What is its main idea most likely about?
choices: The stages of a frog's growth
practice.explain: Headings point at the main idea. A section called How Frogs Grow should be mostly about the frog's growth stages.
